summary: Extends Mobile IPv4 to support mobile networks, where a Mobile Router moves one or more subnets together and its Home Agent keeps them reachable. The Mobile Router hides the movement from nodes behind it, which need no mobility support. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: When a whole small network moves, the devices inside it should not have to know. This RFC lets one device act as the gateway for the others: it registers with its home network as if it were a single travelling host, and the home network sends the traffic for the whole group through it.

what is the mobile network extension type
subtitle: Keeping a whole moving subnet reachable, so the devices inside it need no mobility software.

tldr.problem: Some devices travel together as a group, such as the computers on a bus or a camera tethered to a phone, and the networks they travel on change as they move. Mobile IPv4 handles a single moving host, not a moving network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends Mobile IPv4 with a Mobile Router that carries a whole subnet, a new registration extension that names the prefixes it serves, and a Home Agent that authorises those prefixes, sets up a tunnel and advertises the routes.
tldr.outcome: The hosts inside the moving network keep their addresses and run ordinary IP stacks, because the Mobile Router absorbs the movement and the Home Agent keeps the traffic reaching them.

facts.label: Acknowledgement code values
facts.value: 0 success, 1 invalid prefix, 2 unauthorised, 3 forwarding failed

today: RFC 5177 is a Proposed Standard and was later extended by RFC 6626, which adds dynamic prefix allocation for Mobile IPv4 network mobility. The document addresses mainly the co-located Care-of Address mode, and the extension type 148 with its three sub-types remains the way a Mobile Router names the prefixes it serves.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document describes network mobility extensions to the Mobile IPv4 protocol. The goal is to accommodate mobility scenarios where groups of hosts and routers move homogeneously, as a whole. It is required that all hosts and routers in a Mobile Network be able to run applications connecting to the Internet, and be reachable from the Internet.

A Mobile Network links together a set of hosts and routers. Connecting it to the Internet is ensured at two levels. A Mobile Router is connected on one side to the Mobile Network and on another side to a wireless access system. A Home Agent placed on the home link manages traffic between the Correspondent Node and a Local Fixed Node, a node in the Mobile Network, by means of encapsulating traffic.

A scenario of applicability is a wireless-enabled Personal Digital Assistant and a portable photographic camera linked together by a Bluetooth wireless link-layer technology, sometimes called a Personal Area Network. The PDA plays the role of the Mobile Router and the camera the role of Local Fixed Node. When the camera uploads photographic content to a Correspondent Node server and the Mobile Network moves away, the Mobile Router changes its point of attachment from one cellular access router to another and obtains a new Care-of Address, and the Home Agent encapsulates the application traffic for the correspondent and the camera.

More complex Mobile Networks are easily accommodated by the extensions presented here. Laptop computers used by passengers in a bus, train, ship or plane should all be considered as forming Mobile Networks, as long as they move together.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a phone with a camera attached to it. The camera talks to the phone over a short link, and the phone is the one that moves between cellular towers. The camera does not know or care; the phone takes care of that for it.

sections.title: Overview of the Protocol
sections.content:
The entities sending and receiving the extensions are the Mobile Router and the Home Agent. The Local Fixed Node is relieved from running Mobile IP software and, although it moves with the Mobile Network, its IP stack is not seeing any change in addressing.

Mobility for the entire Mobile Network is supported by the Mobile Router registering its current point of attachment, the Care-of Address, to its Home Agent. The Mobile Router sends an extended Registration Request to the Home Agent, which returns an extended Registration Reply. This signalling sets up the tunnel between the two entities. The prefixes used within a Mobile Network, either implicitly configured on the Home Agent or explicitly identified by the Mobile Router in the Registration Request, are advertised by the Home Agent for route propagation in the home network. Traffic to and from nodes in the Mobile Network is tunnelled by the Home Agent to the Mobile Router and vice versa.

Though packets from a Local Fixed Node placed in the Mobile Network can be forwarded by the Mobile Router directly without tunnelling if reverse tunnelling were not used, these packets will be dropped if ingress filtering is turned on at the access router. The specification addresses mainly the co-located Care-of Address mode. Foreign Agent Care-of Address mode with legacy foreign agents is supported but without optimization, and with double encapsulation being used.

Compared to Mobile IPv4, this document specifies an additional tunnel between the Mobile Router's Home Address and the Home Agent, encapsulated within the normal tunnel between the Care-of Address and the Home Agent. In co-located Care-of Address mode the additional tunnel is not essential and could be eliminated, because the Mobile Router is the recipient of the encapsulated packets for the Mobile Network. All traffic between the nodes in the Mobile Network and the Correspondent Nodes passes through the Home Agent, and the document does not touch on aspects related to route optimisation of this traffic. Multihoming for Mobile Routers is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Only two devices take part in the new signalling: the router that leads the moving group and the home agent that represents it. Everything else, the traffic and the route advertisements, is tunnelled through that pair.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
Terminology for Mobile IPv4 mobility support is defined in RFC 3344, and terminology for network mobility support from an IPv6 perspective is described in RFC 4885. The document adds four terms of its own.

A Mobile Router is a mobile node that can be a router responsible for the mobility of one or more entire networks moving together, perhaps on an airplane, a ship, a train, an automobile, a bicycle or a kayak. A Mobile Network Prefix is the network prefix of the subnet delegated to a Mobile Router as the Mobile Network. The Prefix Table is a list of Mobile Network Prefixes indexed by the Home Address of a Mobile Router, which the Home Agent manages and uses to determine which Mobile Network Prefixes belong to a particular Mobile Router. A Local Fixed Node is a fixed node belonging to the Mobile Network and unable to change its point of attachment.
sections.plainLanguage: The moving group is called a Mobile Network, the address range it uses is a Mobile Network Prefix, and the home agent keeps a list of which prefixes belong to which moving router.

sections.title: The Mobile Network Extensions
sections.content:
In explicit mode, the Mobile Router informs the Home Agent about the Mobile Network Prefixes during registration. The Registration Request contains zero, one or several Mobile Network Request extensions in addition to any other extensions defined by Mobile IPv4. When several Mobile Networks need to be registered, each is included in a separate extension with its own Type, Length, Sub-Type, Prefix Length and Prefix fields, encoded in Type-Length-Value format.

The Type field is 148, the Mobile Network Extension, and the Length is decimal 6. The Sub-Type is 0 for a Mobile Network Request. The Prefix Length is an 8-bit unsigned integer indicating the number of leftmost bits covering the network part of the address contained in the Prefix field, and the Prefix is a 32-bit unsigned integer in network byte order containing an IPv4 address whose leftmost Prefix Length bits make up the Mobile Network Prefix.

The Registration Reply contains zero, one or several Mobile Network Acknowledgement extensions. For implicit mode, the acknowledgement informs the Mobile Router of the prefixes for which the Home Agent sets up forwarding with respect to this Mobile Router. For explicit mode, each Mobile Network is included in a separate extension with its own Type, Sub-Type, Length, Prefix and Prefix Length fields. At least one Mobile Network Acknowledgement extension must be in a successful Registration Reply, to indicate that the Mobile Network Request extension was processed and was not skipped by the Home Agent. A Registration Reply may contain any non-zero number of explicit and implicit mode acknowledgement sub-types, and both can be present in a single reply.

The Acknowledgement extension uses Type 148 and Length decimal 8. The Sub-Type is 1 for an explicit mode acknowledgement and 2 for an implicit mode acknowledgement. The Code field indicates success or failure: 0 for success, 1 for an invalid prefix length, 2 for a Mobile Router that is not authorized for the prefix, and 3 for forwarding setup failed. When the registration is denied with the Code field in the Registration Reply set to the network error, the Code field in the included Mobile Network Extension provides the reason for the failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The moving router lists the prefixes it serves in its registration message, and the home agent answers with one acknowledgement per prefix saying whether it accepted it, and why not if it did not.

sections.title: What the Mobile Router Does
sections.content:
A Mobile Router's operation is generally derived from the behaviour of a mobile node as set in RFC 3344. In addition to maintaining mobility bindings for its Home Address, the Mobile Router together with the Home Agent maintains forwarding information for the Mobile Network Prefixes assigned to the Mobile Router.

A Mobile Router should set the T bit to 1 in all Registration Request messages it sends, to indicate the need for reverse tunnels for all traffic. Without reverse tunnels, all the traffic from the Mobile Network would be subject to ingress filtering in the visited networks. On reception of a successful Registration Reply the Mobile Router processes the registration in accordance to RFC 3344, and then checks for Mobile Network Acknowledgement extensions, creates a tunnel to the Home Agent if it is registered in reverse tunnelling mode, and sets up a default route via this tunnel or via the egress interface when registered with or without reverse tunnelling respectively.

A Mobile Router may operate in explicit mode, where it includes Mobile Network Prefix information in all Registration Requests as Mobile Network Request extensions, or in implicit mode, where it includes no such information and the Home Agent obtains the Mobile Network Prefixes by other means than Mobile IP, for example through static configuration on the Home Agent or from the AAA server. For deregistration the Mobile Router sends a registration request with the lifetime set to zero and without any Mobile Network Request extensions.

Error processing has its own rules. If the Code field of the Registration Reply is set to the value meaning the Mobile Router is not allowed to act as one, the Mobile Router must stop sending Registration Requests with any Mobile Network Prefix extensions to that Home Agent. If it is set to the value meaning a prefix operation error, the Mobile Router must stop sending Registration Requests that contain any of the Mobile Network Prefixes named in the Mobile Network Acknowledgement extension. A Registration Reply with no Mobile Network extensions may mean that the Home Agent does not support Mobile Networks at all, and the absence must be interpreted as that case.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ways of working. In explicit mode the moving router tells the home agent which prefixes it serves every time it registers. In implicit mode the home agent already knows, from its own configuration. The moving router also asks for reverse tunnels so that the packets it sends are not dropped by the visited network.

sections.title: What the Home Agent Does
sections.content:
A Home Agent must support all the operations specified for Mobile Node support, and must support both the implicit and explicit modes for a Mobile Router. For a Mobile Router registering in explicit mode the Home Agent takes six steps: check that the Mobile Network Prefix information is valid, ensure the prefixes are authorised to be on the Mobile Router, create a tunnel to the Mobile Router if it does not already exist, set up a route for the Mobile Network Prefix via this tunnel, propagate the Mobile Network Prefix routes via a routing protocol if necessary, and send the Registration Reply with the Mobile Network Acknowledgement extensions.

If there are any subnet routes via the tunnel to the Mobile Router that are not specified in the Mobile Network extensions, those routes are removed. In the case where the Mobile Node is not permitted to act as a Mobile Router, the Home Agent sends a Registration Reply whose Code field says so. For a Mobile Router registering in implicit mode, the Home Agent performs the last four of those steps once the registration request has been processed successfully. For deregistration the Home Agent removes the tunnel to the Mobile Router and all routes using that tunnel, and ignores any included Mobile Network Request extension.

Two data structures matter. The Registration Table holds the binding information for every mobile node registered with the Home Agent, and the Home Agent must store the Mobile Network Prefixes associated with the Mobile Router in the corresponding registration entry when the registration was performed in explicit mode. The Prefix Table lets the Home Agent authorise a Mobile Router for the use of Mobile Network Prefixes in explicit mode and locate the prefixes associated with it in implicit mode. It may store the Home Address of the Mobile Router along with the prefixes, or, if the Mobile Router has no Home Address assigned, the Network Access Identifier that will be used in dynamic Home Address assignment.

For every Mobile Network Prefix extension in a Registration Request the Home Agent must check the Prefix Table. If the table does not contain at least one entry pairing that Home Address to that Mobile Network Prefix, the check fails. A prefix that fails should carry the code for a Mobile Router that is not authorised; a prefix that passes carries the success code. The Home Agent must then attempt to set up forwarding for each prefix that passed, and a prefix whose forwarding setup failed carries the forwarding setup failed code. If forwarding was successful for at least one prefix the Registration Reply is successful; otherwise the reply says the network prefix operation failed. When the Home Agent is updating an existing binding entry it must check all the prefixes in the Registration Table against those in the new request, and delete any that are missing, disabling forwarding for them as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The home agent does not take the moving router's word for it. It keeps a table of which prefixes belong to which router, refuses any prefix that is not in the table, and tells the router which prefixes it accepted and which it did not.

sections.title: How Traffic Is Forwarded
sections.content:
For traffic to the nodes in the Mobile Network, the Home Agent must perform double tunnelling of the packet if the Mobile Router registered with a Foreign Agent Care-of Address, encapsulating the packet first with a tunnel header whose source is the Home Agent and destination the Mobile Router's Home Address, and then once more with a tunnel header whose source is the Home Agent and destination the Care-of Address. For optimization the Home Agent should encapsulate the packet only once for co-located Care-of Address mode.

When a Home Agent receives a packet from the Mobile Network prefix in the bi-directional tunnel, it must de-encapsulate the packet and route it as a normal IP packet. It must verify that the incoming packet has the source IP address set to the Care-of Address of the Mobile Router, and the packet must be dropped if the source address is not so set.

For traffic from the nodes in the Mobile Network, the Mobile Router encapsulates the packet with a tunnel header whose source is the Mobile Router's Home Address and destination the Home Agent if reverse tunnelling is enabled; otherwise the packet is routed directly to the foreign agent or access router. In co-located Care-of Address mode the Mobile Router may encapsulate one more time with a tunnel header whose source is the Care-of Address and destination the Home Agent.

Nested Mobile Networks, where a Mobile Router allows another Mobile Router to attach to its Mobile Network, are allowed to arbitrary depth. Two issues should be noted. Whenever physical loops occur in a nested aggregation, the protocol neither detects nor solves them, so datagram forwarding may be blocked. And each level of nesting introduces another tunnel header encapsulation, which reduces the usable MTU and adversely affects applications that do not support MTU discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic to the moving group is wrapped up twice when the group registered through a separate foreign agent, and once otherwise. On the way back, the home agent checks that the packet really came from the address the moving router registered.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Mobile Network extension is protected by the same rules as Mobile IP extensions in registration messages. The Home Agent must be able to verify that the Mobile Router is authorized to provide mobility service for the Mobile Networks in the Registration Request before anchoring these Mobile Network Prefixes on behalf of the Mobile Router, and forwarding for prefixes must not be set up without successful authorization. The Mobile Router must be notified when there is a registration failure because it cannot be successfully authorized for prefixes it requested.

All Registration Requests and replies must be authenticated by the Mobile Node to Home Agent authentication extension. When the registration request is sent in explicit mode, all the Mobile Network Prefix extensions must be included before the authentication extension, and these extensions must be included in the calculation of the authenticator value.

The Mobile Router should perform ingress filtering on all the packets received on the Mobile Network prior to reverse tunnelling them to the Home Agent, and must drop any packets that do not have a source address belonging to the Mobile Network. It must also ensure that the source address of packets arriving on the Mobile Network is not the same as the Mobile Router's IP address on any interface. The Home Agent, upon receiving packets through the bi-directional tunnel, must verify that the source addresses of the outer IP header are set to the Mobile Router's Care-of Address, and must ensure that the source address of the inner IP header is a topologically correct address on the Mobile Network, which prevents nodes from using the Home Agent to launch attacks inside the protected network.

If a dynamic routing protocol is used between the Mobile Router and the Home Agent to propagate the Mobile Network information into the home network, the routing updates should be protected with IPsec ESP confidentiality between the Mobile Router and Home Agent, to prevent information about home network topology from being visible to eavesdroppers.
sections.plainLanguage: The home agent must check that the moving router is allowed to speak for those prefixes before it routes anything to them, and both ends must check the source addresses of packets arriving from the moving network, so that a device inside it cannot pretend to be something else.

messages.note: Carries the Care-of Address and the Mobile Network Prefix extensions.

messages.label: Extended Registration Reply
messages.note: Carries the Mobile Network Acknowledgement extensions, one per prefix.

messages.note: Sent to the address of a node inside the Mobile Network.

messages.note: Tunnelled from the Home Agent to the Mobile Router.

messages.note: Delivered on the Mobile Network; the node sees no change in addressing.

fields.desc: Decimal 6 for a Mobile Network Request extension.

fields.name: Prefix Length
fields.desc: Number of leftmost bits that cover the network part of the Prefix.

fields.name: Prefix
fields.desc: An IPv4 address whose leftmost Prefix Length bits make up the Mobile Network Prefix.

viz.caption: THE SUB-TYPE VALUES OF THE MOBILE NETWORK EXTENSION

items.label: Mobile Network Request Extension
items.desc: Sent by the Mobile Router to name a prefix it serves.

items.label: Explicit Mode Acknowledgement Extension
items.desc: The Home Agent's answer for a prefix named explicitly.

items.label: Implicit Mode Acknowledgement Extension
items.desc: The Home Agent's answer for a prefix the Mobile Router did not name.

viz.caption: THE CODE VALUES IN A MOBILE NETWORK ACKNOWLEDGEMENT

items.label: Success
items.desc: The prefix was authorised and forwarding was set up.

items.label: Invalid prefix length
items.desc: MOBNET_INVALID_PREFIX_LEN. The prefix length was zero or greater than 32.

items.label: Not authorised
items.desc: MOBNET_UNAUTHORIZED. The Mobile Router is not authorised for this prefix.

items.label: Forwarding setup failed
items.desc: MOBNET_FWDING_SETUP_FAILED. The Home Agent could not set up forwarding for the prefix.
